name_en: Xiao Qing Gan (Small Green Tangerine Pu-erh)
cultivar: Xinhui tangerine (cha zhi gan) peel with ripe pu-erh from Yunnan's large-leaf
processing: Unripe Xinhui tangerines are washed and hollowed through a small opening, filled with ripe pu-erh, sealed with the peel cap, then dried and kept in dry storage.
harvest_season: Tangerines are picked unripe, in about July to September; the earliest are sold as 'July fruit'. Tea is made separately in Yunnan.
appearance_dry: A small, hard, dark green tangerine shell the size of a large marble or walnut, packed with dark tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear, deep red-brown, as with ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Dark, soft leaf bits inside a softened greenish peel.
taste_profile: Sharp, fresh citrus-peel aroma over the smooth, earthy sweetness typical of ripe pu-erh.

brewing.notes: Weight is for about one whole fruit. Rinse quickly; start with a little peel and add more if you like, since a whole shell can dominate and turn bitter.

vintage_note: Usually sold by the year of the fruit, with new-season stock appearing in late summer. The peel's sharp aroma is the point, so most people drink it within a few years; sellers do also store it dry. Early-picked 'July fruit' is sold as well, so ask when it was picked, and ask where both tangerine and tea come from.
description:
Xiao qing gan is a small unripe tangerine, scooped out and stuffed with ripe pu-erh. It joins two southern Chinese products: Xinhui tangerine peel from Guangdong and fermented tea from Yunnan.

The fruit is picked green while its aromatic oils are high, opened with a small cut, emptied and filled, then dried and rested in a dry warehouse. Good versions use nothing else, with no flavouring or dye.

It brews into a dark, smooth cup with a clean hit of citrus peel. Whole-fruit brewing is the common mistake: it is strong, and peel can take over quickly. Crack it, use part, and keep the steeps short.

The tea inside is usually ripe pu-erh, often from Menghai, and sellers like to mention Xinhui on the pack because the name carries weight. Ask for both places and the fruit's year, and be aware that demand has pulled in earlier-picked fruit.

For something softer, try a larger, later-picked tangerine shell: same idea, more mellow peel.
history: Tangerine peel and tea have a long history together in China, and Xinhui peel has been rated highly since at least the Qing. The small green fruit stuffed with ripe pu-erh is much newer: trade reports date its rise to about 2014, with tangerine pu-erh sales said to have passed 3 billion yuan by 2017. Little is documented about who first made it.
